problem: End-to-end RL/auxiliary-loss agents for Multi-Object Navigation (Multi-ON) are evaluated only in simulation and fail when transferred to a real robot because of the sim2real gap on raw RGB-D sensor data.
motivation: Complex visual-reasoning navigation tasks require mapping and querying seen objects, but their SOTA models have not been tested on physical robots. Feeding the learned policy low-sim2real-gap inputs (occupancy maps) and using classical SLAM and planning for geometry should make transfer robust.
key_idea: A hybrid agent uses classical SLAM (RTABMap) with a D* planner for localization and waypoint navigation, and learns only exploration (an RL policy on the metric EgoMap that outputs a waypoint heatmap) and semantic object detection (a segmentation net); a handcrafted rule switches between exploration and exploitation.
insight: Learned components take only inputs with a small sim2real gap (occupancy EgoMap; segmentation), while geometry is left to classical methods. The real-robot result supports this: the hybrid agent gets 20% success / 43.10 progress, while both end-to-end baselines get about 0% success. The exploration policy also generalizes across domains better than ANS (67.14 vs 52.1 coverage on MP3D after Gibson training), but this is a coverage comparison, not an ablation of the hybrid design. Limiting local plans to 5 subgoals is what made RL training stable.
method: Hybrid map representation: Lidar-based metric occupancy map from RTABMap SLAM (real) or a NavMesh top-down view with fog-of-war (sim), transformed into an egocentric EgoMap, plus a semantic point cloud of detected objects aligned through SLAM localization.

Exploration policy: a recurrent (LSTM) network on the EgoMap predicts a spatial heatmap, masked to unexplored cells; the waypoint is sampled from it. It is trained with RL using a coverage-gain reward (scale 0.01).

Local navigation: D* dynamic planner on the EgoMap, with plans limited to 5 subgoals spaced 0.3 m apart before control returns to the outer loop. This stabilizes RL training and improves real-world robustness.
Object detection and mapping: DeepLabv3 semantic segmentation of RGB-D, supervised with simulator GT masks; detections are back-projected with depth and odometry into the map.

High-level switch: handcrafted rule; if the target is mapped, go to it (exploitation), else explore. Thresholds: 0.7% of pixels to map an object, 5% to trigger Found; the most-pixel detection is chosen when several are present.

setting.backbone: DeepLabv3 segmentation + LSTM exploration policy (trained with RL) + classical RTABMap SLAM and D* planner
setting.training_data: Simulation only, Habitat with Gibson (120 scenes) and Matterport3D (90 scenes); GT object masks used to pre-train the visual encoder; exploration trained with RL on Gibson
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB-D (LoCoBot 160x120, FOV 56°; Multi-ON-Compat 256x256, FOV 79°) + single-ray Lidar + odometry
setting.action_space: Waypoint (x,y) from the exploration policy, converted by the D* planner into low-level discrete/continuous robot motion, plus Found action
setting.privileged: Simulation only: GT navmesh top-down map and perfect localization for the EgoMap, and GT object masks for supervision; none in real-robot tests

numbers.extra: M-ON sensor setup FoV 79°, 256x256; simulation privileged EgoMap

numbers_note: The paper uses Multi-ON (3-object) and reports Progress and PPL, which are not canonical keys. The benchmark name 'MultiON' is used, though it is not written as 'Multi-ON' as listed in the canonical names; mapping to canonical 'MultiON' is assumed. Coverage results (Gibson 88.4, MP3D 67.14) are for exploration only and are not listed above.
results: On the real LoCoBot the hybrid agent gets 20% success and 43.10 progress, while ProjNMap (0% success, 3.00 progress) and ProjNMap+AUX (0 everywhere) fail. In simulation with the LoCo setup on MP3D val it beats ProjNMap+AUX on Progress and Success (63.37 vs 59.97, 50.8 vs 33.4) but has lower SPL/PPL, and in the M-ON setup ProjNMap+AUX is better (Success 48.2 vs 41.8). Exploration coverage on MP3D (domain generalization) is 67.14 vs 52.1 for ANS.
limitations: Real evaluation is tiny (10 episodes, one building), so the real-world results are statistically weak.
The handcrafted high-level switch is sensitive to false-positive detections (e.g., the white cylinder), and path efficiency (SPL) is low.
The paper never tests the end-to-end baselines with real-data adaptation, and it has no ablation isolating each hybrid component.
